articles.title: Cook Political Report shifts 2 Senate races toward Democrats, 1 toward GOP
articles.summary: The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election handicapper, on Tuesday moved Minnesota’s Senate race from likely to lean Democrat, while also moving South Carolina’s Senate seat from likely Republican to lean Republican. The moves give each party something to be hopeful about in the homestretch to the midterms, with Republicans hoping to flip the open…
articles.body:
The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election handicapper, on Tuesday moved Minnesota’s Senate race from likely to lean Democrat, while also moving South Carolina’s Senate seat from likely Republican to lean Republican.

The moves give each party something to be hopeful about in the homestretch to the midterms, with Republicans hoping to flip the open Senate seat in Minnesota being vacated by the retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D), and Democrats suddenly seeing a new opportunity in South Carolina, where Republican Sen. Darline Graham was appointed by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) to replace her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

When Cook moves a race so that it is leaning in one party’s direction, it is just one lane away from being a toss-up.

In another sign that Republicans are struggling to keep hold of states that are usually deep red, Cook also moved the Senate race in Mississippi from solid Republican to likely Republican.

Jessica Taylor, Senate and governors editor at Cook, said in a press release that these races were shifting due to particularly quality candidates on either side.

“In Senate races, the quality of individual candidates can be magnified in ways that defy national trends, especially in midterm years,” Taylor said. “That’s the impetus behind three moves we are making today.”

In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews is running against Graham.

Andrews, a pediatrician, has been campaigning for the seat and raising her profile since May of last year, while Graham has had to rely on her brother’s reputation in Congress while quickly making herself known to voters in the months before the election.

Cook moved that race from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican,” indicating Andrews still faces an uphill climb but may be benefitting both from voters’ dissatisfaction with Republicans nationally, and questions that have arisen about Graham’s strength as a candidate.

In Mississippi, Democrats have grown more bullish. Former President Obama appeared in an ad for Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom last week, and a national Democratic PAC put $1.2 million into television ads for Colom on Tuesday.

Colom, a district attorney, is hoping to unseat Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.). While Mississippi is generally a safe Republican state up and down the ballot, Hyde-Smith is facing headwinds as a Republican and ally of Trump in the Senate amid a national environment unfavorable to the president. Some Democrats — especially Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) — have been saying for months that Mississippi could be competitive and have been urging Democrats to invest there.

Even the few polls done by Democratic pollsters, though, still show Hyde-Smith running ahead of Colom.

In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) has faced attacks from Republicans for not adequately addressing fraud in state social services as part of Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz’s (D) administration. Her Republican opponent, Michele Tafoya, is a longtime television sports reporter whom Flanagan has sought to tie to Trump.

Flanagan is still favored to win , with an 81 percent probability according to Decision Desk HQ.

articles.title: Could France's riots happen here? Experts see parallels in socialism, immigration — and key differences
articles.summary: France riots prompt warnings about Zohran Mamdani, Abdul El-Sayed and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's immigration stances ahead of 2026 midterms.
articles.body: Violent riots sweeping France have exposed a far-left network of communist groups, labor unions and political activists mobilizing around student grievances, raising questions about whether similar political and immigration tensions could ignite unrest on American streets. A Fox News Digital investigation identified 50 organizations involved in France's student protest movement and its broader network of supporters and international amplifiers, including communist and socialist groups, labor unions and political parties. The American parallels extend beyond political rhetoric. Fox News Digital previously reported that agitators at Delaney Hall in Newark used encrypted Signal chats to coordinate transportation, supplies and demonstrations before clashes with federal agents. Santiago Vidal Calvo, a researcher at the Manhattan Institute, singled out New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, arguing that their approaches to immigration enforcement could move the United States closer to conditions he associates with France's crisis. RO KHANNA SPARKS BACKLASH OVER FRANCE RIOT COMMENTS AS CRITIC SAYS HE WANTS TO ‘RIDE THE RAGE WAVE’ "I have absolutely no doubts that if we had Mamdanis or El-Sayeds or AOCs in charge of immigration policy, our immigration landscape would be very different today than what it currently is," Calvo told Fox News Digital. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has made a similar argument, explicitly tying France's violence to the stakes of the 2026 midterms. "France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS — just like the socialist Democrats in America," Johnson wrote on X. "What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way." Johnson argued that a Democratic victory in November would lead to more permissive immigration policies, casting the election as a choice between the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and the approach favored by Democrats. President Donald Trump similarly posted on Truth Social that "migrants have taken over France," urging the country to "CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!" The immigration debate is also playing out directly in the 2026 midterms. In Michigan's closely watched Senate race, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed has made abolishing ICE a campaign position, arguing that the agency cannot be reformed. His Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, has sought to portray El-Sayed as an ideological extremist as the two compete for a seat that could help determine control of the Senate. In New York City, Mamdani signed a February executive order reinforcing sanctuary protections and restricting federal immigration enforcement on city property without a judicial warrant. Both Mamdani and El-Sayed frame their policies as safeguards against abusive enforcement, while critics warn they could weaken immigration controls. The unrest began with students protesting conditions in France's education system before labor unions, political activists and groups with separate grievances joined the movement. Fox News Digital's investigation found that 15 of the 50 organizations identified in the broader network were student or youth groups. Andrew Arthur, a former immigration judge and fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies, described a convergence of frustrations over school funding, rising costs, France's stagnant economy and longstanding tensions surrounding immigration and assimilation. FRANCE IS DEVOURING ITSELF AS SCHOOL RIOTS REVEAL A CRISIS FAR BIGGER THAN BROKEN CLASSROOMS "You've got the simple educational one which is partially economic, you've got the larger economic one and on top of that you have the assimilation issue," Arthur said. But Arthur expressed skepticism that the United States would experience nationwide riots on the same scale, pointing to differences in immigration patterns and assimilation. "Now can we see mass protests like this in the United States? I don't think so," Arthur said, noting that protests over urban ICE operations have not escalated into a comparable nationwide movement. Nathalie Szerman, a Europe-based researcher with the Middle East Media Research Institute (MEMRI), pointed to another potential factor: The demonstrations intensified around the 65th anniversary of the Oct. 17, 1961, massacre of Algerian demonstrators by Paris police. "October 17 is a very symbolic date for the Algerian-ethnic groups," Szerman told Fox News Digital, describing demonstrators memorializing a deadly 1961 crackdown by Paris police on Algerian demonstrators. "The first protest groups were not ideologically aligned with 'political Islam' but were students from immigrant suburbs, driven by education concerns. Agenda-driven, organized 'Political Muslim' groups used the momentum of the protests for their own ends," Szerman said. "It's a lot of things together, the resentment towards France and the political agenda," she said. Alan Mendoza, executive director of the U.K.'s Henry Jackson Society — named for the late Washington Sen. Scoop Jackson — argued that the far-left movement led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon helped encourage broader mobilization ahead of France's next presidential election. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu blamed Mélenchon and his party for the unrest, according to Le Monde, while Mélenchon fired back after Lecornu demanded that LFI "choose a side" between France and the rioters — calling the either-or "detestable." Mendoza warned that similar political tensions could surface in America, citing backlash against socialist New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani from anti-Israel activists who had previously supported him. "What was interesting was the sight of him being turned on by the pro-Palestinian protesters the other day, when he was acknowledging October the 7th, the loss of human life on his radio site, he was turned on by the very hard left people who had helped propel him to power," Mendoza said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "What that shows you is that it is very real a possibility at the hard left who are never satisfied and actually want chaos more than anything else," Mendoza added. Arthur said France's far left can openly champion expansive immigration policies, while American Democrats face a different political reality: They cannot publicly embrace open borders without risking backlash, he argued, pointing to the Biden administration's tendency to portray illegal immigration as a problem it could not control rather than a policy it actively supported. "Riot is to France what football is to the United States," said Arthur. Szerman, however, said comparable unrest was possible despite differences between the two countries. "I definitely think that what's happening in France could happen in the United States," she said, while noting that the more accommodating U.S. education system and different approach to immigrant integration could reduce the severity of any such violence, making a French-style nationwide crisis less likely. Calvo, meanwhile, warned that adopting more expansive immigration policies without adequate screening and integration safeguards could create pressures similar to those he believes contributed to France's unrest. articles.title: On the streets with Dr Oz as surprise fraud crackdown sends daycare directors scrambling
articles.summary: Dr. Mehmet Oz personally confronted staff at two Queens senior care centers over suspicious Medicaid billing, wheelchair charges and attendance records.
articles.body: FLUSHING, N.Y. — Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz confronted employees at two New York City senior care centers over suspected Medicaid fraud, challenging their billing practices as Fox News Digital got an exclusive look at the crackdown in action. Oz, accompanied by senior federal health officials, delivered warning letters to Kent Senior Care and Evergreen Adult Day Care in Flushing, Queens, during a broader fraud crackdown that involved the FBI, the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, the NYPD and other agencies. The letters notified the facilities that their billing practices had raised concerns among federal authorities. The two visits by Oz were part of a broader crackdown in which CMS officials conducted more than 80 visits and delivered warning letters to providers across New York City on Tuesday. Fox News Digital accompanied Oz as he pressed employees about questionable billing records and challenged their explanations for how taxpayer dollars were being spent. DR. OZ NAMES 5 STATES IN FRAUD CRACKDOWN AS TRUMP ADMIN TARGETS MEDICAID ABUSE "The whole experience was suspicious," Oz told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview following the visits. Oz said federal authorities were conducting a broader crackdown that included arrests, search warrants and efforts to stop certain operators from billing Medicaid, although Fox News Digital did not independently witness those enforcement actions at either Queens facility. Kent Senior Care declined comment during a phone call with Fox News Digital on Tuesday. Evergreen Adult Day Care did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Oz questions senior center director: 'We don't believe you' The first stop came around 8:30 a.m. at Kent Senior Care, where Oz entered the facility and personally handed its director a letter from the federal government notifying the business that its billing practices were under scrutiny. FBI LAUNCHES 'MOST WANTED FRAUDSTERS' LIST AS DOJ CHARGES OHIO DEFENDANTS IN $30M MEDICAID SCHEME FOR KIDS "The bills are much higher than they should be," Oz told the director. "The billing is for more people. It doesn't look very crowded here." The director pushed back during the exchange, explaining that it was still early and additional seniors would arrive later in the morning, as Oz questioned whether the facility's Medicaid billing records accurately reflected its actual attendance. The occupancy of the space was 70 persons, according to an observe posted maximum occupancy sign on the wall. "The bills we're getting are as though it's completely full all the time," Oz said. FBI ADDS 2 FUGITIVES TO 'MOST WANTED FRAUDSTERS' LIST AMID HISTORIC $6.5B HEALTHCARE TAKEDOWN: PATEL The director maintained that the facility billed only for seniors who actually attended, and that it required participants to sign attendance sheets. "You're getting this letter from the U.S. Government because we don't believe you," he told the director. During the exchange, Oz also questioned why the center's billing records appeared to reflect seniors attending five days a week when the director acknowledged that many participants typically attended only two or three days. The director insisted the facility billed for actual attendance and said some seniors attended more frequently than others. The confrontation intensified when Oz and other federal officials raised questions about specialized transportation services billed for seniors using wheelchairs. DR OZ SAYS 800 HOSPICE PROVIDERS SUSPENDED IN CALIFORNIA OVER ALLEGED $1B MEDICARE FRAUD SCHEME "I don't see any wheelchairs here," Oz told the director. Fox News Digital observed seniors inside the facility, including individuals using walking aids, but did not see anyone using a wheelchair during the visit. Another official said billing records included charges for specialized wheelchair transportation, raising questions about whether the services had been provided and which company was responsible for submitting the charges. The director said some seniors had mobility difficulties, including those recovering from strokes, and that the facility had wheelchairs available. He also said that workers could have copied information from previous files instead of properly updating the billing codes as it applied to wheelchair use. "Probably he just copy and pasted," the director said. MEDICAID PROVIDER ALLEGEDLY BILLED $165K FOR DEAD PATIENT'S RIDES AMONG FRAUD EXPOSED IN EXPLOSIVE REPORT During the visit, Oz walked over to several mahjong tables set up inside the facility, questioning whether taxpayer dollars were being properly spent on the recreational activities offered through the Medicaid-funded program. "Should the American taxpayers be paying so folks can play mahjong?" Oz asked the director. The director defended the activity, explaining that mahjong helps seniors exercise their fingers, socialize and improve their memory, particularly those experiencing cognitive difficulties. "It's free for them, not free for the taxpayers," Oz responded. "Is that what our federal tax dollars for Medicaid is supposed to go to? Or is it life-saving heart surgery? Or, you know, new therapies for cancer?" Oz raises concerns over seniors entering without signing in Oz raised additional concerns about the facility's attendance records after observing seniors entering without signing in, despite the director's insistence that participants were required to document their attendance. "People were just walking in there without signing anything," Oz said. "And then after I showed up and he saw what we were doing with my team, he started collecting these documents to be signed." Oz said the apparent inconsistencies raised further questions about whether the facility's attendance records accurately reflected the services being billed to Medicaid. Fox News Digital also witnessed several seniors enter Kent Senior Care without immediately signing attendance sheets. Additional seniors who arrived later were instructed to sign in. Social adult day care programs can provide eligible seniors with structured activities, supervision, meals and social support. Medicaid reimbursement depends on applicable program rules, individual eligibility and documentation of services provided. TREASURY HAILS SUCCESS OF ANTI-FRAUD PROCESS THAT FLAGGED AND PREVENTED $99 MILLION IN PAYMENTS TO DEAD PEOPLE At the second stop, Evergreen Adult Day Care, Oz confronted a floor manager over another set of billing discrepancies before examining the facility's attendance records. The manager told Oz that approximately 200 seniors attended the facility on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, compared with about 150 on Tuesdays and Thursdays, although it was unclear whether those figures represented total daily attendance or the number of seniors present at one time. But Oz questioned those numbers after walking through the facility and observing significantly fewer people. "So I look at maybe 25 people in the whole space now," Oz said. The manager disputed that estimate, explaining that some seniors were participating in classes while others had left to shop, visit a pharmacy or attend medical appointments. "The numbers don't seem to add up," Oz responded. Oz also questioned the manager about wheelchair-related billing, asking how many participants used wheelchairs. TRUMP'S WAR ON FRAUD EXPANDS AS TREASURY LAUNCHES NEW SITE WITH WHISTLEBLOWER INCENTIVES The manager initially indicated that none did before acknowledging that a small number of seniors used them. "But you said there weren't any, were you?" Oz pressed. He subsequently discussed the apparent discrepancy with other federal officials accompanying him. "I'm struck by how few people are here as well," Oz said. "This makes me wonder how they sustain these billing levels." The visit took another turn when Oz examined the facility's attendance books, which he said contained "fraud." Fox News Digital observed sign-in sheets that appeared to contain names entered for Oct. 22, and Oct. 23, dates that had not yet occurred at the time of the visit. The entries dated Oct. 22 and Oct. 23, both after the visit, raised questions about whether the facility was documenting attendance in advance, although Fox News Digital could not immediately establish whether the entries were completed attendance records or advance schedules. Oz alleges organized crime ties to NYC Medicaid fraud Oz said federal authorities believed organized criminal networks were exploiting the Medicaid-funded programs by offering seniors money to attend facilities and then billing the government for services that were not actually provided. Oz alleged that individuals he described as being connected to the "Chinese mafia" were paying some seniors between $1,000 and $1,200 to participate in fraudulent billing arrangements, though the administrator did not identify a specific criminal organization or provide supporting evidence during the interview. Oz said the federal government had identified significant spikes in billing across the industry and claimed that annual spending on the programs had approached $1 billion. "We know from the billing here that there's no way this business is running in the way that they claim to be running without something being wrong," Oz told Fox News Digital. "Is it an innocent mistake? A hundred times in a row, I don't think so." Oz alleged that proceeds from fraudulent Medicaid billing schemes were being used to finance other criminal activities, including money laundering and human trafficking, although Fox News Digital had not independently verified those connections or established any such link to the two facilities visited. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's really a clubhouse for crime," Oz said while describing the alleged broader scheme. He said fraud accelerated during the COVID-19 pandemic and criticized the previous administration for failing to address what he described as rapidly rising spending and suspicious billing. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul acknowledged the crackdown on Tuesday, calling it part of a "massive effort to combat fraud and abuse" in Medicaid and confirming that state health officials had joined federal and state law enforcement in targeting suspected fraud at social adult day care programs. While Oz personally delivered warning letters to the two Queens facilities, state, local and federal law enforcement officials were simultaneously conducting searches at other locations across New York City as part of the coordinated crackdown. Specific details about the facilities targeted, individuals involved and evidence recovered were not immediately available as the investigations remained ongoing.

articles.title: Oxfam analysis finds Peru’s richest captured 42 percent of all new wealth
articles.summary: Only 1.4 percent of all new wealth created between 2019 and 2025 went to the poorest 50 percent, report finds.
articles.body:
The top 1 percent in Peru captured 42 percent of all new wealth generated between 2019 and 2025, an analysis by the nonprofit group Oxfam has found.

The report, released on Tuesday, highlights growing inequality in the South American country and raises questions about how the government is addressing deepening social divisions.

“Economic inequality in Peru has remained stubbornly high for decades. And when people feel that the same people always win, that nothing changes and nothing can change, inequality starts to look less like an injustice and more like the natural order of things,” said Alejandra Alayza, the executive director of Oxfam in Peru.

“That is a dangerous kind of fatalism, and we must tear it down.”

The nonprofit told Al Jazeera in an email that the 42 percent figure represents an increase from the 2000 to 2019 period, when the top 1 percent captured about 39 percent of all new wealth.

Just 1.4 percent of new wealth from 2019 to 2025 went to the poorest 50 percent of the country’s population, according to the group.

Experts warn the trend bodes poorly for public faith in government and democratic institutions .

Oxfam worked with the Institute for Peruvian Studies, a think tank in Lima, to publish a report this month on Peruvians’ perceptions of inequality in their country.

The groups found that 84 percent of Peruvians believed their country is governed by powerful interests that shape politics to their benefit. More than 75 percent also said that wealthy corporations and individuals avoid paying their fair share of taxes.

The survey also suggested that public opinion was in favour of action to address the issue.

About 70 percent of respondents said they want the government to do more to reduce inequality, which a majority felt had limited access to services such as healthcare, employment, education and justice.

“The undeniable scale of public support for action to reduce inequality leaves no room for complacency,” Alayza said.

“Inequality is not a force of nature; it is made by political choices. And different choices can build a different Peru.”

Peru’s rising inequality has been accompanied by a period of political turmoil, particularly in the presidential palace.

A stream of probes, scandals and impeachments has led to Peru being governed by nine presidents in the last 10 years.

The latest, right-wing President Keiko Fujimori, was sworn into office in July after a narrow race that saw voting delays and heated recriminations among the leading candidates.

Experts believe powerful interests have found opportunity amid the political tumult.

“It’s sort of a paradox. How can you have such a rotation among elites but still have a relatively narrow political-criminal-business elite that holds a lot of power? I think both things are true in Peru,” Will Freeman, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, a US-based think tank, told Al Jazeera.

Part of the political upheaval has come from clashes between the presidency and Peru’s powerful Congress, which has the power to impeach executive leaders on the basis of “moral incapacity”, an ambiguous term.

The repeated leadership shakeups have weakened Peru’s democracy, according to analysts.

In December 2022, for instance, then-President Pedro Castillo announced that he would illegally dissolve Congress in response to repeated attempts to impeach him.

His subsequent removal and arrest prompted widespread protests. The government of Castillo’s successor, Dina Boluarte, implemented a months-long crackdown on the demonstrations that rights groups say included widespread abuses for which there has been little accountability.

In the years since, the Peruvian government has also taken steps to weaken judicial oversight and hollow out anticorruption watchdogs.

The nonprofit Freedom House, which measures political freedom in countries around the world, ranked Peru as “free” in 2022. But its ranking dropped the following year to “partly free”, in light of the deadly clashes between security forces and protesters.

In its 2026 report, Freedom House maintained that Peru was only “partly free”, citing in part the denial of full political rights to certain groups, including Indigenous peoples.

“High-profile corruption scandals have eroded public trust in government, and the weakening of judicial independence has impacted the country’s governing bodies,” the nonprofit said.

Powerful interests, both licit and illicit, have taken advantage of those changes.

“The groups themselves are unstable and fluid,” said Freeman. “And yet, I think Peruvians are right to conclude that, generally, they are wielding outsized influence in defence of their own commercial interests or political power rather [than] in service of some kind of general welfare.”

articles.title: Mamdani says El-Sayed win is of ‘critical importance’ to New York City
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Tuesday expressed his support for Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and said his victory in the competitive Senate race would signal openness to a new political future in the country. During a press conference, the mayor was asked by a reporter about whether he would back…
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Tuesday expressed his support for Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and said his victory in the competitive Senate race would signal openness to a new political future in the country.

During a press conference , the mayor was asked by a reporter about whether he would back El-Sayed and other Democrats running in the midterm elections.

“I think that his victory and the victory of Democrats across this country is of critical importance to our city because what it also indicates is a willingness to chart a new course in Washington that has working people at the heart of it,” Mamdani said.

The mayor identified parallels between his administration’s goals and El-Sayed’s campaign objectives, specifically citing the Democratic nominee’s pushback on super PAC spending in politics and advocacy for issues like “Medicare for all” and bringing down the cost of living.

“Those are concerns that ring true for Michiganders. They’re also concerns that ring true for New Yorkers,” Mamdani continued.

The democratic socialist, who won the mayoral race last year, added that his focus remained on the city’s five boroughs.

El-Sayed has pushed back on attempts to characterize him as a democratic socialist, instead labeling himself as a progressive populist candidate focused on addressing affordability concerns.

The Michigan Democrat is running in a tight race against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.).

The Cook Political Report , a nonpartisan election forecaster, rates this contest as a “toss up.” Polls from Fox News and Marist University last month found El-Sayed with a narrow lead over his GOP opponent.

During a fiery debate earlier this month, the two candidates lobbed personal attacks at one another.

El-Sayed pressed the Republican over his loyalty to President Trump amid rising energy costs tied to the U.S.’s military operations against Iran. Rogers alleged that his opponent, who is Muslim, had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and appeared to suggest El-Sayed could have terrorist family relatives — claims the Democrat forcefully disputed.

The opponents will face off again on Wednesday in a debate hosted by WXYZ-TV.

articles.title: Sabato’s Crystal Ball moves nearly 3 dozen House races in Democrats favor
articles.summary: Nonpartisan election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball is moving 28 House races in Democrats’ direction with just two weeks until the midterms. When adding up the seats Crystal Ball says are either safe, likely or leaning toward one party, the new projections put Democrats above the 218 needed for a House majority. In other words, Democrats…
articles.body:
Nonpartisan election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball is moving 28 House races in Democrats’ direction with just two weeks until the midterms.

When adding up the seats Crystal Ball says are either safe, likely or leaning toward one party, the new projections put Democrats above the 218 needed for a House majority. In other words, Democrats could lose every race rated as “toss-up” and still win if Crystal Ball’s ratings prove accurate.

Crystal Ball Managing Editor Kyle Kondik wrote in his analysis that it would be a “shock” if Democrats did not win a decently sized House majority.

“At this point not only would it be a shock if Republicans held the House, but it would also be a surprise if Democrats did not at least exceed the tiny-sized majorities of the last three Congresses,” Kondik wrote.

The forecaster, a division of the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics, moved six races from “safe Republican” to “likely Republican,” six from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican” and one race from “leans Republican” to “toss-up.”

It moved nine more races from “toss-up” to “leans Democratic” and six from “leans Democratic” to “likely Democratic.”

Among the most notable shifts are in Iowa, where Crystal Ball now rates three out of the state’s four House seats “leans Democratic.” Republicans currently hold all four of the Hawkeye State’s seats in the lower chamber.

Crystal Ball also moved two GOP-held seats in Arizona, the 1st and 6th Congressional Districts, to “leans Democratic.”

The forecaster also pushed some seats further into the Democrats’ column that their party already holds but are easier to flip following Republican mid-decade redistricting efforts.

That includes the open Texas 35th Congressional District , which Crystal Ball moved from “leans Republican” to “toss-up,” and Rep. Don Davis’s (D) bid to hold on in North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, which went from a “toss-up” to “leans Democratic.”

Of the 15 seats Republicans recently redrew with more GOP-friendly lines, just three are rated “safe Republican.”

Kondik also identified a handful of races where Democrats could upset Republicans in districts not expected to be competitive.

Potential upsets include the reelection of bids of Reps. Victoria Spartz in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, Mike Flood in Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District and Jeff Van Drew — a former Democrat who switched parties in 2020 — in New Jersey’s 2nd Congressional District. All three of those are among the six races shifting from “safe Republican” to “likely Republican.”

“[Democratic] candidates just swamped Republicans in third quarter fundraising reports released late last week, blunting a GOP outside spending edge,” Kondik wrote. “Seemingly each day brings a new report of some new concern for Republicans in a race that wasn’t on the radar earlier in the cycle.”

articles.title: Italy unleashes military response to violent riots as France faces a reckoning of its own
articles.summary: Videos show police forced to retreat as rioters overwhelm officers in Paris and Milan, prompting France and Italy to announce military deployments.
articles.body: Italy is moving to deploy 500 troops with expanded police powers following a weekend of violent riots, taking a more direct military approach to public security than France, where weeks of unrest have prompted authorities to bolster their security response. Videos of unrest in France and Italy flooded social media on Saturday and Sunday, showing violent clashes between demonstrators and police amid burning buildings and looted storefronts. At multiple points during the chaos, police attempting to contain the violence were forced to retreat. In Paris, for instance, roughly a dozen officers confronted several hundred demonstrators but were unable to make arrests, using rubber-bullet launchers and grenades to keep advancing rioters at bay as they made a gradual retreat. Italian police in Milan, meanwhile, made a similar retreat as hundreds of young rioters threw explosive firecrackers, metal barriers and glass bottles at them in their attempt to occupy a public square. Though France is escalating its response now, demonstrations have been ongoing in the country since last month, with many schools being burned and ransacked by rioters. MACRON JETS OUT OF RIOT-TORN FRANCE FOR GULF TRIP AS POLITICAL PRESSURE MOUNTS A Fox News Digital investigation found that socialist groups, Islamic advocacy organizations and environmental activists were involved in the French riots, which financial analysts estimate caused over $1 billion in damages. Videos from the unrest also showed demonstrators waving foreign flags, including Palestinian flags in France and an Albanian flag during the violence in Milan. Italian media reported that many first and second-generation migrants were among the rioters in Milan. WHO'S WHO: INSIDE FRANCE'S 'CHAOS INC.' FRANCHISE OF COMMUNIST GROUPS, LABOR UNIONS AND GLOBAL ACTIVISTS With another wave of riots planned for this coming weekend and authorities bracing for more violence, France and Italy are turning to their armed forces to reinforce security after days of rioting. France’s gendarmes, essentially military police officers, assisted in containing last weekend’s riots. The nation’s interior minister announced on Tuesday that the military would be increasing its presence in anticipation of further rioting. FRANCE'S MASSIVE INTEL FAILURE SPARKS RESIGNATION OFFERS AMID DAYS OF RIOTING "We will ⁠deploy the Sentinelle force, ​obviously ‌as a substitute ‌to interior security ‌forces ... mostly to free police and gendarmes in their mission to maintain order," he ‌told France’s legislature. France has upcoming presidential elections, with some political observers viewing the migrant-heavy riots as an electoral boon for Marine Le Pen, the most popular right-wing candidate. The country’s deputy prime minister explained that the police would be granted police powers, providing some insight into the role they could play in squaring off against rioters.

articles.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
articles.summary: The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the latest tariffs on the country and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.

The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August.

The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.

The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".

The White House has been contacted for comment.

Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.

Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.

"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.

The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.

That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".

The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.

Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.

It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.

Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency.

"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.

The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada.

"The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.

The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.

It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year.

Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".

articles.body:
Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton’s (D) mother called her a “liar” in a new ad, as her brother labelled the video “a despicable low” on Tuesday ahead of the state’s elections in November.

“I love my daughter, but when I saw her lying about her opponent — it is not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy has a serious problem. She is a liar,” Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, appeared to say in the ad.

“She lies about her past. She says she grew up living in a tent. None of that is true. She’s lied her entire life. My daughter needs help, and she can’t help you if she needs help herself,” Arthur continued.

“People can change, but first they have to tell the truth. And my daughter still isn’t doing that. Don’t vote for people who lie. Don’t let her become your governor. If you think she’ll make your life better, you’re fooling yourself. It will only get worse,” she concluded.

The ad appears to be a campaign-style video, but it is unclear who is backing or paying for it.

Senate Majority PAC (SMP) announced Tuesday that it will spend the money on television and digital ads through Election…
articles.body:
A top Democratic super PAC is launching a $1.2 million ad campaign in the Mississippi Senate race, adding the deep-red state to its list of targets as the party seeks to flip the Senate in November.

Senate Majority PAC (SMP) announced Tuesday that it will spend the money on television and digital ads through Election Day supporting Scott Colom (D), who is challenging Trump-backed Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.).

SMP’s first 30-second ad focuses on Colom’s work as a district attorney, portraying him as a candidate willing to “fight corruption in both parties” while criticizing Hyde-Smith as a “do-nothing” senator.

“It is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels,” SMP spokesperson Lauren French said in a statement.

Nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted the Mississippi Senate race from solid Republican to lean Republican — another sign that Republicans may have a tougher fight than usual to hold this seat.

Hyde-Smith’s campaign disputed the competitiveness of the race, while tying Colom to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

Campaign spokesperson Nathan Calvert told Politico, “Chuck knows what Mississippians know, Scott Colom is too liberal” for the Magnolia State, while noting “It took Chuck Schumer and his Super PACs thirteen months to run a single ad for Scott Colom.”

Calvert went on to attack Colom for supporting “transgender surgeries for children, men in women’s restrooms and locker rooms, open borders, and higher taxes,” while asserting “Team Cindy is confident that voters will reject this radical agenda at the ballot box on November 3rd.”

The announcement comes days after former President Obama appeared in a campaign ad for Colom, urging Mississippi voters to back the Democrat while highlighting his record as a prosecutor.

“Mississippi, it’s time for a change. That’s why you need to send Scott Colom to the U.S. Senate,” the former president said in the ad.

The spending is the latest effort by the Schumer-aligned super PAC to expand the Senate map beyond traditional battleground states. The group is also spending in Kansas, Alaska, Texas and Iowa, all of which President Trump won by double digits in 2024.

Mississippi is an especially difficult state for Democrats. Trump carried it by 23 percentage points in 2024, and the deep red state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

articles.title: Trump deflects on potential Vance endorsement
articles.summary: President Trump did not say whether he would endorse Vice President Vance for a 2028 presidential bid on Tuesday after Vance said on Monday that he believed his boss would back him if he were to run. “He’s a very talented person and he’s a very good person,” Trump said when asked alongside Vance in…
articles.body:
President Trump did not say whether he would endorse Vice President Vance for a 2028 presidential bid on Tuesday after Vance said on Monday that he believed his boss would back him if he were to run.

“He’s a very talented person and he’s a very good person,” Trump said when asked alongside Vance in the Oval Office.

“I don’t think we’ve ever talked about it,” the president said, turning to Vance.

“No, sir. I said that too,” Vance chimed in.

“Who would believe that?” Trump said, “I don’t talk about it with him. He doesn’t talk about it [with me]. It’s early.”

“We have to get through the midterms. We’ll see how it goes,” he added

Vance said in an interview with 2Way on Monday that he thinks Trump will endorse him if he runs in 2028.

“I think I would get his endorsement, but I also think there’s something to be said for people actually running their own race,” the vice president said. “And because the president’s endorsement is so dispositive, you could absolutely see a scenario where the president says, ‘You know what? We need to let like this race play out and not preemptively prejudge the results.’”

“Like sometimes you know media scrutiny, pressure, policy. I can be terrible at it, and that is the sort of thing that maybe you know, so I don’t know,” he continued.

Vance did note that he has not spoken with Trump about potentially running for president, adding, “if I run, I think the president would endorse me. But I also haven’t talked to him about it yet.”

The vice president has said repeatedly that he is focused on helping Republicans defend their majorities on Capitol Hill ahead of the midterms but has been floated as a top 2028 Republican contender .

articles.body: Vice President JD Vance said he isn't sure if he'd receive President Donald Trump's endorsement "right out the gate" if he were to run for president in 2028. Vance expressed that uncertainty during a Monday interview with journalist Mark Halperin on his platform 2Way. The interview aired just weeks before the midterm elections, as Republicans and the White House are focused on maintaining control of Congress. Vance emphasized that his top priority was the midterms and said he wasn't certain that a 2028 presidential run was in his future. However, he said, "I think if I run, the president will endorse me." "No, I don’t think it’d be weird," Vance said. "Again, I think I would get his endorsement, but I also think there’s something to be said for people actually running their own race, and because the president’s endorsement is so dispositive, you could absolutely see a scenario where the president says, ‘You know what? We need to let, like, this race play out and not, like, preemptively prejudge the results.'" "That’s the person they say, ‘Okay, if Trump is with a guy, that must mean that the elites are against that guy," Vance said. "I think that Trump’s endorsement just carries more weight than any political endorsement in history because of that. Obviously, the voters are gonna decide. articles.body:
Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex, says he’s hoping to patch things up with his family and that working on a reconciliation is “the most important thing” to him.

The 42-year-old British prince opened up about where things stand with his family in an interview published Tuesday in GQ . Harry has reportedly been estranged for years from his father, King Charles III, along with his older brother, Prince William.

Harry and his wife, Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, stepped away from their full-time royal family duties in 2020.

Asked if the “complicated relationship” with his father and sibling is something he grieves, Harry replied, “Yes, of course. I think from a family perspective, again: another massively relatable issue for so many people. There’s sibling disagreements, there’s broken relationships between kids and their parents, kids and one parent.”

“That continues to come up with me the whole time by people that I speak to , s o I know how relatable it is. That’s probably why there’s so much fascination,” Harry, who’s promoting his MasterClass focused on dealing with grief, told the magazine.

“And then people maybe look at us and go, ‘How are you going to work it out?’ And then, maybe, how I see you’re going to work it out, maybe that will help me work my stuff out,” he said.

“And some people don’t want it to work out. I want it to work out,” Harry said.

Pressed on his response about having a desire to mend his relationship with his family, Harry said, “Of course I do. Again, with everything else that’s going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile.”

Harry and Meghan recently returned to the United Kingdom — moving back to London in August with their two children after spending six years in California.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar's daughters show up at scene of DC raid as rumors swirl about embattled rep's whereabouts
articles.summary: Isra Hirsi was spotted entering Ilhan Omar's D.C. home under cover of darkness as Capitol Police were called to the residence later that evening.
articles.body: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. has not been seen in public since a pre-dawn raid of her Washington, D.C. residence last week — but Fox News Digital spotted her daughters descending on the home in recent days. Isra Hirsi pulled black sedan into the driveway of the home under the cover of darkness Saturday night and stepped out of the vehicle carrying a bag with both hands. She walked directly into the front door of the same home that was swarmed by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents a week prior. "What's your problem?" Hirsi said to Fox News Digital after getting out of her car. Just two days later, a young teenage girl believed to be Omar's second daughter also was seen entering the home with a woman that appeared to be her caretaker. ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION The daughters arrived on the scene roughly a week after the house was raided by federal agents. Omar also has a son who is the only immediate family member of Omar's that Fox News Digital has not seen arrive at their home in D.C., since the federal search where her phone and passport were reportedly seized. The same night Omar's eldest daughter was captured entering the home, U.S. Capitol Police (USCP) — whose jurisdiction is typically limited to U.S. Capitol building and grounds, but extends to protecting members of Congress and their families — showed up on the congresswoman's street. Omar shares her three children with Ahmed Hirsi, who she ceremonially married in 2002 and legally married in 2018. During the time before her legal marriage to Hirsi, she was legally married to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, who is allegedly her brother, from 2009 until 2017 — during which time Omar's youngest daughter was born. She married political consultant Tim Mynett in 2020. Throughout the week after the raid, Mynett has emerged from the home intermittently, mostly to walk the family’s Golden Labrador Retriever dog, Teddy. He has defended his wife to Fox News Digital, saying he has "no concerns" about the investigation. He also snapped when asked about unsubstantiated rumors that the congresswoman had fled the country. "You guys are annoying the hell out of the neighbors around here, man," said Mynett. Omar's eldest daughter, Isra Hirsi, is controversial in her own right. The 23-year-old activist and graduate of Barnard College — a Columbia University affiliate — was arrested at Columbia and later suspended from the school in 2024 after participating in the school’s now-infamous anti-Israel tent encampment, which lasted for two weeks until it was dispersed by NYPD. ILHAN OMAR'S HUSBAND SNAPS OVER RUMORS SHE FLED US AFTER FEDERAL IMMIGRATION FRAUD RAID She also co-founded the U.S. Climate Strike in 2019, part of a global movement that organized student walkouts of class as they demanded the passage of the far-left Green New Deal and a switch to 100% renewable energy. Despite its name, the group didn’t stop at advocating for "green" energy policies. It also demanded universal healthcare, student debt relief, stronger union organization and advocated for giving land back to Native Americans. Hirsi has also railed against capitalism publicly on social media. Omar's sister, Sahra Noor, did not show up for a scheduled stop on her book tour in Minnesota last week due to a "family emergency," according to the book store hosting the event. Three sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that Noor voluntarily spoke with federal investigators last week. Omar’s home was raided by HSI, the chief investigatory body of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), at around 6:00 a.m., last Monday. Sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that the agency executed a search warrant in relation to an immigration fraud probe. Specifically, investigators are probing whether the congresswoman and/or her father falsified information when filling out her citizenship paperwork. Border Czar Tom Homan revealed over the weekend that if the allegations are proven, they could lead to Omar’s denaturalization. The New York Times reported that about a dozen people, including Omar’s relatives, have been subpoenaed in the case. Omar has not responded to repeated requests for comment from Fox News Digital, but she has reacted publicly to the raid on social media. REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES "This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," she said in a statement posted to X hours after the raid. For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back. Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies." In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital last Tuesday, Vice President JD Vance said the investigation is not politically motivated. "We don't want to be like the Biden administration. We never want to be like that — where they would allow the law to go after their political opponents," he said. "And if justice requires something else be done, then, of course, we'll take a step when we have to."

articles.title: CNN threatens Trump’s DOJ with further legal action over Air Force One blocks
articles.summary: CNN is threatening President Trump’s Department of Justice (DOJ) with further legal action if the White House continues blocking the network from performing its duties in pool rotation. In a letter to the DOJ this week, CNN’s attorney Ted Boutrous wrote “these efforts to retaliate and discriminate against CNN based on the content of its…
articles.body:
CNN is threatening President Trump’s Department of Justice (DOJ) with further legal action if the White House continues blocking the network from performing its duties in pool rotation.

In a letter to the DOJ this week, CNN’s attorney Ted Boutrous wrote “these efforts to retaliate and discriminate against CNN based on the content of its news coverage are mistaken, counterproductive, and unlawful,” the outlet reported.

Boutrous argued that certain White House spaces the West Wing has attempted to block CNN from “belong not to any particular president or administration but to all Americans.” He added that “CNN and other members of the press serve as surrogates for the public when covering the White House.”

CNN was one of three outlets the president sought to ban from the White House last month before a federal judge ordered access for the journalists be restored.

Trump’s decision sparked a brief boycott by other TV networks, which rotate duties pooling coverage of the president’s daily activities and statements.

CNN is part of that rotation and has been blocked on several occasions from boarding Air Force One or entering other White House spaces the TV pool representative typically has access to.

The president has long warred with CNN, accusing the network of publishing “fake news” and insisting he has a right to keep them from covering his White House.

A judge in Washington, D.C., is currently weighing whether a temporary injunction he handed down last month restoring CNN’s access to the White House grounds covers pool coverage specifically.

articles.body:
Meghan McCain, former Sen. John McCain’s (R-Ariz.) daughter, decried what she called a “dastardly” political ad featuring Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton’s (D) estranged mother.

“This is a dastardly ad. It never should have been created. Shame on whatever consultant firm created this,” McCain wrote on social platform X Tuesday.

McCain’s response came amid a wave of backlash surrounding the political ad, in which Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, called her daughter a “liar.”

“She lies about her past. She says she grew up living in a tent. None of that is true. She’s lied her entire life. My daughter needs help, and she can’t help you if she needs help herself,” Arthur said before telling voter to not let “her become your governor.”

The clip appears to be part of a campaign-style ad, but it is unclear who is backing or paying for it. When asked about the video, a spokesperson for her Republican gubernatorial opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, told The Hill, “We don’t know what happened between Amy and her mother.”

The spokesperson continued, “But we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor.”

Acton said in a 2019 interview with The Vindicator that while living with her mother in the aftermath of her parent’s divorce, she experienced sexual abuse, neglect and a period of homelessness.

Eventually, charges were filed against Acton’s stepfather, and she moved in with her father and relatives.

Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, responded in a press release to the ad on Tuesday, stating it was “not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point.”

“After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died,” Stearns added.

articles.title: Reporter’s Notebook: A Democratic majority could expose the limits of the progressive agenda
articles.summary: Hakeem Jeffries faces a balancing act between DSA-backed progressives and moderate majority makers if Democrats flip the House in the midterms.
articles.body: "You made me promises. Promises.Knowing I'd believe.Promises. Promises.I knew you'd never keep." — Promises, Promises by Naked Eyes "I am a supporter of Medicare-for-all," declared Minnesota’s Democratic nominee for Senate, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, D. "I'm going to get there with my friend Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. And we are going to power map the s--t out of the U.S. Senate and figure out how to build power for the things that we know that we deserve and the things that we need." Hard-left progressive House and Senate candidates like Flanagan are pitching Medicare-for-all. The abolition of ICE. The Green New Deal. An arms embargo for Israel. And a $25 an hour minimum wage. Flanagan is in a race with Republican Senate nominee Michelle Tafoya to succeed retiring Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn. The race favors Flanagan. However, it’s not a done deal that she wins. But Democratic Socialist candidates for the House like Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Melat Kiros in Colorado, along with Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York probably will. Come January, they will prospectively represent Democratic strongholds where progressive ideas are popular. MEET THE FAR-LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT IN 2026 MIDTERMS But if Democrats win either the House or Senate, it won’t be because voters pulled the lever for Kiros in Denver or Avila Chevalier in Harlem. They’ll win because Democrat Cait Conley defeated Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., in Dutchess County, north of New York City. Maybe because voters cast their ballots for Democrat Brian Poindexter in Wooster, Ohio, rather than Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio. Democrats could flip the House if Democratic nominee Christina Bohannan appeals more to voters in Davenport, IA than Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa. This brings us back to the progressive agenda. Democrats might win the House and or the Senate. But Valdez and Kiros aren’t the "majority makers." Candidates like Poindexter and Conley are. And if they’re elected to the House, it’s doubtful that moderates from swing districts can support progressive ideas like the Green New Deal or Medicare-for-all. It’s about the math. And it’s more than likely that Democrats will need the voters of those moderate "majority makers" from battleground districts to enact those policies. That’s to say nothing about needing 60 yeas in the Senate to crack a filibuster – even if Democrats do marshal a slim majority there. And, if something extreme did get through both bodies of a potentially Democratically-controlled Congress, President Trump would like veto it. THE BLUE WAVE LOOKS REAL UNTIL YOU LOOK A LITTLE CLOSER It is said that you campaign in poetry but you govern in prose. The left has pushed a lot of progressive poetry with their agenda items of late. They’ll tout the opportunity to enact some of those policies if Democrats win the majority. However, the reality of advancing any of that into a legislative reality is slim. The progressive ideas may energize the base. But the Democratic base is sure to feel let down if Democrats can’t make good on some of their campaign promises. We’ve seen this before. A party promises voters the moon in the midterm elections. Then struggles to make good on those promises. Republicans won the House in 1994 for the first time in four decades with the 10-point "Contract With America." The document promised to cut spending and reduce influence in Washington. But in the end, the House and Senate only approved a few of the items. President Clinton vetoed others. In 2006, House Democrats campaigned on drawing down the war in Iraq. They captured the House. Congress began defunding the war effort. But it took several years, much to the dismay of party activists who demanded an immediate pullout. In 2010, Republicans won back control of the House, gaining a record 63 seats. The goal was to reduce spending and repeal and replace ObamaCare. It never happened. In fact, some Republicans are still trying to unwind ObamaCare today. CARVILLE SAYS HE'D RATHER REPUBLICANS KEEP THE HOUSE THAN DEMOCRATS WIN BY FIVE SEATS, HELD 'HOSTAGE' BY DSA This is all about exciting the base. And then figuring out how to govern. What candidates promise on the campaign trail rarely morphs into a legislative reality. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is reportedly in discussions with DSA-backed candidates to secure legislative commitments before some of their candidates will back him in a potential race for Speaker. That said, political observers would find it hard to believe that Democrats would balk at promoting Jeffries, making him the first Black House Speaker in American history. There’s a chance Democrats could face infighting if the party fractures between moderates and progressives. Imagine for a moment that Democrats do have the House and intend to bring a Medicare-for-all bill to the floor. The House must first adopt a rule which governs how the House debates that measure on the floor. Would a moderate Democrat like Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., oppose the rule (provided she wins reelection)? After all, Gluesenkamp Perez voted for GOP procedural measures earlier this year, igniting an internal Democratic firestorm. However, those votes may have been good matches for her battleground district. But voting aye on a procedural plan for a controversial, progressive political initiative won’t work in Gluesenkamp Perez’s district. That’s why the progressive agenda may already be dead in the water. If Democrats do win the House and Jeffries clasps the Speaker’s gavel, his role will be different. He needs to manage his entire caucus. So appealing to the hard left doesn’t work. He must also hear out the moderates. And certainly the majority makers. For instance, Jeffries isn’t pushing the Medicare for all scheme. HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY "I haven't co-sponsored the Medicare for all legislation that has been introduced over the last several years. I do think we need to figure out how to fix our broken healthcare system and then build something better once we repair the damage that has been done," said Jeffries. That’s a natural stance for a national political leader. Jumping feet first into such a nettlesome issue might not be sound politics. Especially since you must also address the concerns of the moderate majority makers. But Jeffries may have an out that all Democrats can unify around: investigations of the Trump administration. Since President Trump began his term, Jeffries has promised to hold its officials to account. Jeffries has called out Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. Ridiculed Attorney General Todd Blanche. Blasted Vice President JD Vance. Spoken about alleged corruption by the Trump family. Democrats are also campaigning as a foil to the Trump Administration. Their base will demand action via investigations, too. That certainly resonates with the progressive base. And, even moderates who may be the majority makers. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But it isn’t a $25 an hour minimum wage. It’s not the abolition of ICE. It’s not the Green New Deal. Democrats probably won’t get what they want legislatively if they attain the majority. Those are just the political realities. But they may be able to rack some points with investigations. Those would reflect the political realities as well.

articles.title: Trump says he’s spent $300M in midterms so far
articles.summary: President Trump said on Tuesday that he had already spent over $300 million in the midterms to help Republicans as the GOP looks to stave off major losses in both chambers of Congress. “…I am pleased to announce that, having to do with the Most Important Midterm Elections in our Country’s History, I have spent,…
articles.body:
President Trump said on Tuesday that he had already spent over $300 million in the midterms to help Republicans as the GOP looks to stave off major losses in both chambers of Congress.

“…I am pleased to announce that, having to do with the Most Important Midterm Elections in our Country’s History, I have spent, or will be spending, over 400 Million Dollars by Election Day,” the president wrote in a post on Truth Social .

“More than 300 Million Dollars has already been spent on Advertising, Direct and Indirect Voter Contact, Rallies, Rally Arenas, Telerallies, Get Out the Vote Programs, Election Integrity, and more,” Trump added.

MAGA Inc., the president’s super PAC, and Trump’s affiliated No Going Back PAC Inc. and Safety & Affordability PAC Inc. are expected to report their monthly federal campaign spending on Tuesday. None of the groups had reported their monthly campaign finance filings at the time of publication.

The president has previously vowed to spend between $400 million and $500 million to support Republicans in November. MAGA Inc. ended August with $415 million in the bank, and Republicans have pressed his political groups to spend heavily, especially in the Texas Senate race where Trump-endorsed Republican Ken Paxton is in a tight race against Democrat James Talarico.

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) forecasts that Democrats have a 77 percent probability of taking back the House and a 56 percent of taking back the Senate as Republicans contend with Trump’s low approval ratings and high cost of living expenses.

MAGA Inc. and the president’s affiliated groups have primarily spent money in competitive Senate races in states like Texas, Alaska, Ohio and Michigan. They’ve also poured money into battleground seats and even some Republican-leaning House districts.

Republicans have a major fundraising advantage compared to their Democratic counterparts, buoyed further by the Supreme Court’s decision striking down federal limits on coordinated campaign spending between political parties and campaigns.

Still, Democrats have still raked in major amounts of cash, including $60 million raised from Talarico’s campaign alone this past fundraising quarter. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) brought in $33 million from his campaign while Michigan Senate Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed raked in nearly $31 million.

articles.body:
Rep. Jasmine Crockett insisted she is supporting fellow Texas Democrat James Talarico in his ongoing Senate bid, arguing her down ballot focus will ultimately help him.

“I’ve endorsed him 100 times,” Crockett said during a stop in Houston on the first day of early voting Monday, the Houston Chronicle reported .

Talarico, who defeated Crockett in the Texas Democratic primary, is now facing off against state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) for a seat in the Senate. In August, when asked if she would campaign with Talarico, Crockett told CNN she would focus on “ campaigning down ballot ” instead.

On Monday, Crockett doubled down on her down ballot agenda, according to the Chronicle, saying during the campaign event “the top of the ticket is going to benefit” from her efforts to boost turnout for Democrats in local races, such as Letitia Plummer’s and Alisa Simmons’s county judge bids.

In May, the Democratic lawmaker launched the “Fuel Individual Rights Everywhere,” or FIRE, leadership political action committee. Later that month, all five Texas candidates backed by her PAC won their respective primary runoffs.

The Washington Post reported last month that Talarico was not among the 14 candidates Crockett’s PAC had endorsed. Its latest list of endorsements , which has over 50 candidates, still does not include Talarico.

When faced with criticism over Talarico’s absence from the list, Crockett reposted her concession to Talarico on social platform X .

“Y’all are corny! I keep receipts. I’ll be happy when people either give a damn about FACTS or news media goes back to the news instead of deciding to ride the tabloid lane. NOW FOR THE 1000th time maybe write an article about KEN F*in PAXTON. Y’all all sound like corny groupie a– OPS!” she wrote on X last month.

Three recent polls released last week showed Talarico narrowly leading Paxton two weeks ahead of Election Day. No Democrat has won statewide Texas election since 1994.

articles.title: Acton responds to ad, says personal attacks ‘a lifelong pattern’ for Ramaswamy
articles.summary: Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D) accused Republican rival Vivek Ramaswamy of a “lifelong pattern” of personal attacks after a political ad surfaced online in which her estranged mother called her a “liar.” Acton, who has publicly discussed suffering abuse as a child, suggested Ramaswamy’s campaign was behind the video and criticized him for using…
articles.body:
Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D) accused Republican rival Vivek Ramaswamy of a “lifelong pattern” of personal attacks after a political ad surfaced online in which her estranged mother called her a “liar.”

Acton, who has publicly discussed suffering abuse as a child, suggested Ramaswamy’s campaign was behind the video and criticized him for using her family history just two weeks before Election Day.

“I won’t normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something I’m complaining about, who today just released an ad using my birth mother, who I was removed from at the age of 12 for severe abuse and neglect, and sexual abuse,” Action told Spectrum News on Tuesday.

“This is a lifelong pattern with my opponent,” she added, pointing to similar personal attacks Ramaswamy levied towards Nikki Haley’s daughter during a GOP debate in the 2016 presidential election.

It remains unclear who produced or paid for the video, which does not identify a sponsor. Ramaswamy’s campaign has not confirmed any involvement, but spokesperson Connie Luck defended the ad’s criticism of Acton.

“We don’t know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth,” Luck said in a statement.

Acton’s campaign also responded Tuesday with its own ad, titled “Abuse,” featuring her brother, Phil Stearns, describing the abuse they endured growing up and ripping Ramaswathy for using it as a talking point in the campaign.

“Shame on Vivek,” he says. “It’s the contempt he has for Amy. It’s the contempt he has for Ohio. He’s not fit to lead.”

The minute-long video, which began circulating on social media on Monday, features Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, calling her daughter a liar and urging voters to avoid casting their ballots for her.

“I love my daughter, but when I saw her lying about her opponent — it is not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy has a serious problem. She is a liar,” she says in the ad.

“People can change, but first they have to tell the truth. And my daughter still isn’t doing that. Don’t vote for people who lie. Don’t let her become your governor. If you think she’ll make your life better, you’re fooling yourself. It will only get worse,” she added.

articles.title: The Senate map expands (again): From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Bridget Bowman looks at the latest red state Democrats are making a play for in the battle for the Senate.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Bridget Bowman looks at the latest red state Democrats are making a play for in the battle for the Senate. Plus, Jane C. Timm provides an overview of the key secretary of state races on the midterm ballot. — Adam Wollner Democrats jump into the Mississippi Senate race By Bridget Bowman Two weeks out from Election Day, Senate Democrats’ top super PAC is launching a new ad campaign in the Mississippi Senate race, the latest example of the party seeking to make inroads in traditionally Republican states in the fight for the majority. Senate Majority PAC announced a $1.2 million ad campaign in the state through Nov. 3, beginning with a 30-second spot that boosts prosecutor Scott Colom as a Democrat who will “fight corruption in both parties” and casts GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith as a “do-nothing” incumbent. “Senate Majority PAC has been watching this race closely, and it is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels,” Lauren French, the super PAC’s spokesperson, said in a statement, also noting that the group will be advertising on TV and digital platforms. The group, which is aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., has been shifting its focus to deep-red states amid President Donald Trump’s sinking approval ratings. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win control of the Senate, which means flipping multiple states Trump won handily in 2024. Mississippi is the reddest state the super PAC has jumped into so far — Trump won it by 23 points two years ago. A Democrat has not won a Senate race in Mississippi since 1982. Senate Majority PAC is also spending in Kansas, which Trump won by 16 points, as well as other states the president carried by double digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas. The group’s GOP counterpart, Senate Leadership Fund, is also airing ads in those states, with the exception of Mississippi. In addition, SLF has poured money into South Carolina to shore up GOP Sen. Darline Graham as she seeks a full term in office, and into Nebraska, where Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts faces a challenge from independent Dan Osborn. Read more → Battleground state voters weigh who should oversee their elections By Jane C. Timm Voters in a handful of swing states will decide next month who will hold critical election oversight power during the next presidential contest. Arizona, Georgia, Michigan and Nevada — which have all been critical battlegrounds in recent national elections — have secretary of state races on the ballot. A role that was once under the radar, these offices have become much more high profile amid a constant drumbeat of unfounded election fraud claims from President Donald Trump and his allies. Secretary of state races in 2022 in particular received outsize national attention in the wake of Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 results. In that election cycle, Democrats spent more than $71 million on campaign ads for secretary of state races across the country, while Republicans spent nearly $15 million, according to data from AdImpact. This year, spending is down across the 26 secretary of state races on the ballot: Democratic campaigns and outside groups have spent $16.6 million on ads, compared to more than $5 million by the Republicans. But the emphasis is once again on the narrowly divided swing states that are expected to be at the center of the 2028 presidential map. In Arizona and Nevada, two Democratic incumbents are running against far-right Republicans who have pushed election conspiracy theories. Meanwhile, open-seat contests in Georgia and Michigan have drawn Republicans who are casting themselves as moderates looking to increase trust, while Democrats paint them as Trump allies who will undermine confidence in elections. Former Kentucky Secretary of State Trey Grayson, a Republican, said GOP candidates vying to be their states’ top election officials face a difficult balance: They must appeal to Trump’s ardent supporters, who believe there is widespread fraud, without alienating independents. “You know what happened; you know what safeguards exist in your state and across the country. In the battlegrounds, it’s almost like you have to go full throttle” on election denialism, he said. “But then in doing so, you make it very hard, if not impossible, to win it in the fall.” Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.
