articles.title: Why do the US midterms matter for Trump and Congress?
articles.summary: Republicans and Democrats jockey for control of Congress, which will set course for Trump’s final two years in office.
articles.body:
The United States midterms on November 3 are dominating national and international headlines.

The stakes of the election are high. The midterm race will determine which party controls the US Congress, and in turn, shape the direction of Trump’s final two years in office. It will also decide key state and local positions.

But notching big wins in the midterm election may not be enough to shake up the balance of power in Washington, DC.

To understand the implications of this year’s midterm election and what may come next, Al Jazeera has put together this simple primer.

Here’s why the US midterms matter at the federal level.

Battle for the US House of Representatives and US Senate

Midterm elections fall at the halfway point of a president’s term, meaning the executive office will not be on the ballot.

Front and centre will be the battle for control of Congress. Two chambers make up the US legislature: the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Because members of the House serve two-year terms, all 435 seats in the chamber are up for election on November 3. However, most races are already considered formalities, with a clear frontrunner.

That leaves only a handful of races — about 50 — to decide who will win the House majority.

While subject to change, nearly every reputable election prognosticator has predicted that Democrats will win control of the House, some by as many as 15 seats.

The Democrats have a slimmer chance of winning a majority in the Senate, however.

That chamber has only 100 seats. But because senators have staggered six-year terms, only 35 seats are up for election. Only about a dozen of those races are considered competitive.

Still, Democrats have seen their odds of seizing the Senate increase, as the number of competitive races has grown.

Left-wing candidates have made inroads in deep-red states like Texas and Kansas, creating more opportunities for the Democratic Party to claim a Senate majority this election cycle.

Because the US vice president breaks ties in the Senate, Democrats would need 51 seats to control the chamber.

Congress passes laws and approves federal budgets. But even if a party secures a majority in both chambers of Congress, it may not be enough to control the country’s legislative agenda.

Laws can pass by a simple majority in the House, but they typically need a supermajority of 60 votes in the Senate to overcome a process known as the filibuster . That process can allow a minority group to stall legislation indefinitely, barring a supermajority.

Therefore, unless a party wins more than 60 seats in the Senate, most legislation will still require at least some level of bipartisan support to pass.

Even if legislation passes both chambers, the president can veto any bill that comes across his desk. Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds supermajority in both the House and the Senate.

Achieving the broad bipartisan support needed to overcome a presidential veto is exceedingly rare.

The last time it happened was in January 2021, during Trump’s first term. At the time, the US president had lost the 2020 election, and he saw his support from Republican lawmakers dissipate when he attempted to veto a defence spending bill.

Still, there are instances when bipartisan support overcomes presidential objections. A bill to increase the housing supply passed both the House and Senate with veto-proof majorities earlier this year, despite Trump’s stated opposition .

So what happens if Republicans maintain control of Congress?

Republicans currently hold two majorities in Congress, with 53 seats in the Senate and 218 in the House.

With Trump in the White House, that means the party has held a so-called government “ trifecta ” over the last two years, with three levers of power under its command.

The Republican majorities in Congress have helped Trump pass some of his signature legislation, including surging funding to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and cleaving back some forms of publicly funded healthcare as part of a sweeping 2025 tax bill.

But Republicans’ numbers have not been enough to pass Trump’s entire legislative wishlist. Notably, he has been unable to pass his signature federal voter identification law, dubbed the “ SAVE America Act “, amid Democratic opposition.

There have also been a handful of issues where Republicans have defied Trump, particularly on tariffs . A few Republicans have also voted to assert congressional authority over the US-Israel war with Iran.

If the Republican Party maintains control of both the House and Senate in November’s race, its majorities could continue to help Trump’s legislative agenda. But there is an important caveat.

Lawmakers will be keeping an anxious eye on voter sentiment as the 2028 elections approach. With Trump unable to seek a third term, some Republicans may have more appetite to publicly oppose the lame-duck president during the next two years, in order to boost their election prospects.

If Republicans maintain control of the Senate but lose the House, they would still be able to help Trump confirm his nominees for key federal roles.

Hundreds of federal positions require approval from a simple majority in the Senate, including roles in the judiciary, including Supreme Court justices.

The party in control of Congress, with a few exceptions, can determine what legislation is brought to a vote and when.

But for Democrats, the most significant outcome of winning a majority in one or both chambers would be the ability to block Trump from legislating his agenda over the next two years.

That said, analysts expect a Democrat-led Congress to take a largely defensive stance, batting down Trump’s proposals.

Going on offence — and passing their own legislative agenda — will be far more difficult, even if the party wins a majority in both the House and Senate. Democrat-led laws would still face Trump’s veto power.

However, holding majorities would help Democratic members slip policy priorities into “need-to-pass” funding legislation. The spectre of a government shutdown could pressure Republicans to pass budget bills, even if they do not agree on all the terms.

Democrats can also bring topics to a vote to force congressional Republicans to oppose popular policies or simply take a public stance on divisive issues.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has laid out a 100-day plan for if Democrats take control of the chamber. Topping the agenda are votes on Trump-backed healthcare funding cuts, asserting congressional authority over the US-Israel war with Iran and rolling back Trump’s tariff programme.

Those issues have split the Republican base and would pose thorny dilemmas for lawmakers already posturing for the 2028 vote.

As Trump rallies on behalf of Republicans in the run-up to November’s vote, he has repeatedly expressed concern that Democratic control of Congress could lead to one eventuality: his third impeachment.

Trump was already impeached twice during his first term. “If we don’t win, they’ll end up impeaching me,” he told a rally in Durant, Oklahoma, in early October.

If Democrats do take control of the House or the Senate, they will take over leadership of dozens of committees. Through those committees, they can launch investigations — with subpoena power — into an array of subjects.

Some Democrats have already said probing allegations of Trump family corruption will be a top priority.

House lawmakers can also introduce articles of impeachment and ultimately vote to impeach federal officials, including the president, with a simple majority.

However, the Senate would need to vote to convict the official with a two-thirds majority before they can be removed from office.

Perhaps more significantly, if Democrats win control of the Senate, they would be able to block the confirmation of Trump appointees in key roles during his final two years in office.

So what will change on the war with Iran and the economy?

A Democratic surge is likely to signal discontent with the Trump administration, but there will not be a swift, tangible change on many of the issues that have defined the election season.

For example, if Democrats secure both majorities in Congress, they could assert their leverage to seek to address affordability issues, drilling into topics like housing, healthcare and the cost of living.

But they can do little to immediately change the myriad factors that led to the high price of petrol and groceries. Any gains would most likely be hard-fought, slow-coming and incremental.

The same is true for the US-Israel war with Iran.

Under the US Constitution, only Congress can declare war, something it has not done since World War II. Presidents have long used various legal arguments to circumvent that constitutional requirement.

Most recently, the Trump administration argued that the US-Israel war with Iran did not require authorisation from Congress because the president has a duty to protect the American people.

Trump has also argued that the war has started and stopped several times, each time renewing the 60-day window he has to receive Congress’s authorisation.

To reassert Congress’s authority to declare war, Democrats could pass a legally binding “war powers resolution” to rein in Trump, but they would need two-thirds support to overcome the presidential veto.

Even if a resolution were able to overcome the veto, experts say it is unclear how the US judiciary would respond if Trump were to flout Congress’s will.

Still, Democrats could use control of Congress to attempt to stifle any funding for the war.

articles.title: Who is Ana Reyes, federal judge Trump called a ‘crazed lunatic’?
articles.summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes shot down the Justice Department’s (DOJ) demand to not participate in a key hearing on Monday on the future of East Potomac Park, which President Trump wants to turn into a championship-style golf course. The Trump administration has alleged that Reyes is biased after she yelled at a government attorney…
articles.body:
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes shot down the Justice Department’s (DOJ) demand to not participate in a key hearing on Monday on the future of East Potomac Park, which President Trump wants to turn into a championship-style golf course.

The Trump administration has alleged that Reyes is biased after she yelled at a government attorney last week over hundreds of trees being cut down at the park without extra notice.

Reyes is overseeing a lawsuit brought by a preservationist group and golfers challenging Trump’s desire for the championship-style golf course.

“The judge on the case is a crazed lunatic whose courthouse tapes will reveal, may be insane?” Trump wrote on Truth Social early Monday.

Here’s what you need to know about Reyes:

Born in Uruguay, Reyes was raised in Louisville, Ky. She attended Transylvania University, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts in 1996, eventually going on to earn her law degree at Harvard University in 2000.

In 2001, Reyes spent time as U.S. Appellate Judge Amalya L. Kearse’s law clerk. From 2001 to 2023, she was a litigation attorney for Williams & Connolly LLP, a D.C.-based law firm. According to the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia’s website, while at the firm, her work was centered around “international litigation, representing foreign governments, foreign government officials, and multinational companies.”

In February 2023, former President Biden appointed Reyes to her current role on the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. Upon entering the position, she became the first openly LGBTQ official to serve as an Article III judge in Washington, D.C.

According to a press release from the Biden White House from April 2022, Reyes is also the first U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia’s Hispanic woman. The Biden White House touted her LGBTQ and Hispanic identity in the release.

Reyes was confirmed by the Senate in a tight 51-47 vote, with the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) the only Republican to vote in her favor.

Reyes’s current clash with the current administration is not the first time she’s butted heads with the federal government under Trump.

In March 2025 , she blocked implementation of an executive order from the president effectively restricting transgender people from serving openly in the military. Reyes barred Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and other military officials from putting the order or new policy effectuating it in place.

Reyes also found that Trump broke the law by firing multiple inspectors general at the beginning of his second term, but also that she couldn’t put them back in their jobs.

articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Kyle Kennedy, a granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy and Ethel Kennedy, died last month at 42, according to her obituary .

Kennedy died Sept. 21 at her home in Massachusetts. Her cause of death has not been disclosed.

Kennedy’s death came six years after she suffered a severe spinal cord injury that left her with long-term paralysis. She became an advocate for people living with disabilities, including testifying at the Massachusetts State House during a hearing on discrimination against people with disabilities in healthcare.

According to her obituary, she was also a passionate advocate for more equitable elementary education and charter schooling.

Kennedy has two sons with her former husband, Liam Kerr. According to Page Six , the couple married in 2012 in a high-profile ceremony attended by Taylor Swift and her then-boyfriend, Conor Kennedy, the bride’s cousin.

articles.title: Trump says Ilhan Omar could go to jail or be deported, calls her ‘a disgrace to our country’
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said Ilhan Omar could face jail in addition to deportation, calling her "a disgrace" amid a federal immigration fraud probe.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Rep. Ilhan Omar could face jail in addition to deportation, calling the Minnesota Democrat "a disgrace to our country" as she faces a federal investigation into allegations involving her citizenship. Trump made the remarks inside the Oval Office during his fraud incentive program announcement, responding to FOX Business correspondent Edward Lawrence’s question about whether a problem with Omar’s age could lead to her deportation. "Well, she could be. She could also go to jail," Trump said. "You know, they keep talking about deportation. No, she could go to jail." ILHAN OMAR SHOULD BE JAILED, DEPORTED IF CITIZENSHIP FRAUD PROVEN, TOP HOUSE REPUBLICAN SAYS The president did not identify a specific criminal charge or present new evidence against Omar during the exchange. "This is just my opinion," Trump added, before calling the congresswoman "a very dishonest person" who "hates our country." OBAMA BACKS ILHAN OMAR AMID PROBE, ACCUSES TRUMP ADMIN OF 'APPALLING' TARGETING IN LENGTHY STATEMENT His comments come after border czar Tom Homan said Omar could lose her citizenship and be deported if investigators prove immigration fraud. Federal agents searched her Washington, D.C., home Oct. 12, seizing her cellphone and other possessions. The investigation centers on allegations that Omar or her father misrepresented her birth year on immigration paperwork. The disputed timeline concerns whether she was a minor when her father became a U.S. citizen in 2000 and qualified for citizenship through him, or was already 18 and needed to apply separately. HOMAN SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD BE STRIPPED OF NATURALIZATION, DEPORTED IF IMMIGRATION FRAUD IS PROVEN Omar has denied wrongdoing. She and other Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., have denounced the investigation as political persecution targeting a prominent Trump critic ahead of the midterm elections. Speaking Saturday on "The Big Weekend Show," Homan said the outcome would depend on the evidence. DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’ "Of course, if you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody. We’ve done it before," Homan said. "And certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen." Homan said Omar would be held to the same standards as anyone else, while declining to discuss the specifics of investigators’ findings. HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION INVOLVING ILHAN OMAR, SAYS HE KNOWS 'THINGS ARE GOING ON’ "I’m not going to get ahead of the bureau or HSI, but I’ve been told they have a strong case, and we’ll let the evidence lead where it leads," he said. During Tuesday’s exchange, Trump also attacked Omar’s criticism of the United States, questioning why she sought to tell Americans how to run the country after coming from Somalia. ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS "Then she comes over here, and she says that she wants to tell us how to run America," Trump said. "She wants to tell us how to run the United States of America." He also criticized her assertions of constitutional rights and called her election to Congress "amazing." TRUMP RALLY CROWD CHANTS 'DEPORT' AS PRESIDENT RIPS ILHAN OMAR AFTER FEDERAL RAID "She’s a disgrace to our country," Trump said. The president ended the exchange by saying he hoped Omar would receive fair treatment. "I hope they treat her fairly," he said. articles.title: Acton’s brother slams Ramaswamy in new ad: ‘Not fit to lead’
articles.summary: The brother of Amy Acton, the Democrat running in Ohio’s gubernatorial race, denounced GOP nominee Vivek Ramaswamy after a new video circulated online featuring Acton’s estranged mother calling her a liar and urging Ohioans to vote against her daughter. In a new ad for Actor, Philip Stearns blamed GOP candidate Vivek Ramaswamy for the video…
articles.body:
The brother of Amy Acton, the Democrat running in Ohio’s gubernatorial race, denounced GOP nominee Vivek Ramaswamy after a new video circulated online featuring Acton’s estranged mother calling her a liar and urging Ohioans to vote against her daughter.

In a new ad for Actor, Philip Stearns blamed GOP candidate Vivek Ramaswamy for the video featuring his and Acton’s biological mother.

“Shame on Vivek,” Stearns said. “It’s the contempt he has for Amy. It’s the contempt he has for Ohio. He’s not fit to lead.”

It is not yet clear who paid for the campaign-style video, as the clip did not disclose a financial sponsor. A spokesperson for Ramaswamy’s campaign defended the clip in a statement shared with The Hill earlier Tuesday, though the campaign did not take responsibility for the video.

“We don’t know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor,” the spokesperson said.

The Hill has reached out to Ramaswamy’s campaign for comment on this new ad.

Acton had disclosed in a 2019 interview that she experienced sexual abuse, neglect and a period of homelessness while living with her mother following her parents’ divorce. Acton’s stepfather was charged with raping Acton when she was 12 years old.

He pleaded not guilty and was indicted by a grand jury in 1978, according to the AP – and, after no-showing a court hearing, he was a fugitive until 1981.

In an interview with Spectrum News on Tuesday afternoon, Acton said she would not “normalize” her opponent’s use of her estranged mother’s words against her.

“The words our leaders use matter, and I think it’s going to take courage right now from all of us to stop normalizing this sort of rhetoric,” she told the outlet.

Democratic officials denounced the campaign video on Tuesday, with Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey condemning the clip as “a disgusting and shameful political attack from Vivek Ramaswamy” in a social media post .

“The people of Ohio deserve so much better than the likes of Vivek Ramaswamy,” she added.

Additionally, the daughter of the late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.), Meghan McCain, slammed the ad as “dastardly.”

“It never should have been created,” she wrote on social media . “Shame on whatever consultant firm created this.”

articles.title: Musk endorses Paxton in Texas Senate race
articles.summary: Tech mogul Elon Musk has formally endorsed Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race after bankrolling his campaign for several weeks. The tech billionaire and one-time trillionaire has spent more than $150 million on Paxton’s candidacy as the lone donor to Texas PAC, a political action committee supporting Paxton. In a post to the…
articles.body:
Tech mogul Elon Musk has formally endorsed Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race after bankrolling his campaign for several weeks.

The tech billionaire and one-time trillionaire has spent more than $150 million on Paxton’s candidacy as the lone donor to Texas PAC, a political action committee supporting Paxton. In a post to the social platform X — which Musk owns — Tuesday, Musk encouraged Texans to get out and support the Texas Attorney General.

“The fate of Texas and America is at stake. Vote for @KenPaxtonTX today,” Musk wrote.

Musk was one of Trump’s biggest donors in 2024, spending at least $250 million to help send him back to the White House. Despite a falling out with the president in the spring of 2025, Musk is back in the political mix and bankrolling Republicans in the midterms. Musk is also a Texas resident, having moved from California to Austin in 2020. Both Tesla and SpaceX are headquartered in Texas.

Paxton finds himself in a tight race with state Rep. James Talarico (D) in a matchup that is key to which party will control the Senate.

While Texas is a traditionally Republican state, one which President Trump won by 14 points in 2024, the GOP is increasingly concerned about the possibility of losing a Senate race in the Lone Star State for the first time since 1988. Preventing that from happening comes with a big price tag.

The two parties have spent more than $500 million on ads in the Texas Senate race, with more than $350 million coming from Republicans, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

But while Musk’s money may help Paxton get on the air, outside spending receives less favorable ad rates on TV than spending from campaigns, as required by federal law. So while Republicans account for 74 percent of ad spending in Texas, according to AdImpact , the party accounts for just 58 percent of actual broadcast airings as of Monday.

Talarico has raised record amounts as a candidate, with a $64 million third quarter haul — the most any Senate candidate has raised in that period in recorded history. That figure far outpaces what Paxton’s campaign has raised.

The barrage of GOP money into Texas has done little to move the polls. Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, showed Talarico leading Paxton by 3.3 points at the end of August in its polling average. As of Tuesday, Talarico still leads Paxton by 2.2 points after hundreds of millions in Republican ad spending.
